description: QUIC decomposed. The first new general-purpose transport since TCP. UDP-based to traverse middleboxes that drop unknown L4 protocols. Encryption is mandatory and integrated (no plaintext like TCP+TLS). Streams multiplex independently — no TCP-style HOL. Connection migration survives IP changes. Packet numbers are independent of stream offsets. The protocol Google built then shepherded through IETF.

sub_mechanisms.name: QUIC_over_UDP
sub_mechanisms.definition: QUIC packets are UDP datagrams. The QUIC protocol logic + reliability + congestion control runs in user space (typically).
sub_mechanisms.why: TCP can't be modified — middleboxes ossified its semantics. UDP is opaque to middleboxes — any new transport over UDP can do what it wants. Trade-off: must reimplement reliability + congestion control in user space.

sub_mechanisms.name: connection_ID
sub_mechanisms.definition: Each QUIC connection has connection IDs (one per direction). Subsequent packets carry the connection ID; receiver identifies the connection without relying on the 5-tuple.
sub_mechanisms.why: Connection survives IP changes. Mobile client switches from Wi-Fi to cellular: 5-tuple changes; with TCP, connection drops; with QUIC, packets keep flowing because connection ID is unchanged.

sub_mechanisms.name: encrypted_long_header
sub_mechanisms.definition: Initial QUIC packets use a long header containing version, connection IDs, packet number. Header is partially encrypted; payload fully encrypted with TLS 1.3 keys.
sub_mechanisms.why: TLS 1.3 is baked into QUIC. Version negotiation happens in the long header. After handshake, packets use the short header (just connection ID + packet number).

sub_mechanisms.name: encrypted_short_header
sub_mechanisms.definition: Post-handshake packets: 1-byte fixed header + connection ID + packet number + encrypted payload. Minimal overhead.
sub_mechanisms.why: After handshake, no need for the long header's overhead. Short header is ~10 bytes vs ~25 for long header. Per-packet efficiency for the common case.

sub_mechanisms.name: stream_frames
sub_mechanisms.definition: QUIC's data unit. Each stream frame: stream ID + offset + data. Multiple stream frames can appear in one packet.
sub_mechanisms.why: Streams multiplex independently. Frame's stream ID + offset uniquely identifies the data position. Different streams can be in different packets; loss of one packet only affects the stream IDs in that packet.

sub_mechanisms.name: per_stream_reliability
sub_mechanisms.definition: Each stream is reliable independently. Loss of stream A's packet retransmits only stream A's data; streams B-Z continue delivering.
sub_mechanisms.why: Solves TCP's HOL blocking. Per-stream reliability is what HTTP/2 needed but couldn't get from TCP. The single biggest QUIC architectural win.

sub_mechanisms.name: packet_number_independent_of_data
sub_mechanisms.definition: QUIC packet numbers monotonically increase per packet (not per byte like TCP sequence numbers). A retransmitted packet gets a NEW packet number.
sub_mechanisms.why: TCP's same-sequence-number-for-retransmit makes RTT calculation ambiguous (was the ACK for the original or the retransmit?). QUIC's monotonic numbers give unambiguous RTT measurement — better congestion control input.

sub_mechanisms.name: ACK_frame_with_ranges
sub_mechanisms.definition: QUIC ACKs are SACK-like by default: report ranges of received packet numbers. Builds in the SACK functionality TCP added as an extension.
sub_mechanisms.why: Selective ACK without the legacy of optional support. Sender always gets precise loss info. Native selective recovery without negotiation.

sub_mechanisms.name: 0RTT_data
sub_mechanisms.definition: After a previous connection, client caches the server's transport parameters + TLS PSK. On reconnect, can send application data with the first packet.
sub_mechanisms.why: Zero handshake latency for repeat visits. Critical for mobile + frequent-reconnection patterns. Same replay concerns as TLS 1.3 0-RTT.

sub_mechanisms.name: connection_migration
sub_mechanisms.definition: When client's IP/port changes (mobile network change), client sends a new packet with the existing connection ID from the new address. Server verifies path then continues.
sub_mechanisms.why: Mobile devices roam between networks constantly (Wi-Fi to cellular, cellular tower changes). TCP would drop; QUIC continues. The defining mobile-friendly property.

sub_mechanisms.name: path_validation
sub_mechanisms.definition: Before accepting a new connection migration, server sends a challenge packet to the new client address; verifies the response.
sub_mechanisms.why: Without verification, attackers could redirect traffic to themselves by spoofing migration. Challenge-response prevents this — attacker must control the new path. Standard cryptographic challenge.

sub_mechanisms.name: amplification_limit
sub_mechanisms.definition: Before path validation, server cannot send more than ~3x the bytes client sent. Limits DDoS reflection potential.
sub_mechanisms.why: Without this, an attacker could spoof a client's IP, send small QUIC handshake, server responds with huge certificate chain to victim. 3x cap means amplification ratio is bounded. Network-friendly default.

derivation_rules.name: UDP_substrate_avoids_middlebox_ossification
if: a new transport runs over UDP
then: middleboxes treat it as opaque and don't constrain its evolution
derivation_rules.why: TCP packets are deeply inspected by middleboxes (firewalls, IDS, NATs); they reject anomalous TCP. UDP has minimal middlebox parsing — datagrams pass through. QUIC chose UDP precisely because middleboxes can't (yet) interfere.

derivation_rules.name: per_stream_reliability_eliminates_HOL
if: streams are reliable independently of each other
then: loss on one stream doesn't block others
derivation_rules.why: TCP+HTTP/2's HOL blocking comes from TCP's single-stream reliability. Per-stream reliability in QUIC: stream A's lost packet retransmits affect only stream A's progress. Streams B-Z keep delivering data immediately.

derivation_rules.name: connection_ID_enables_migration
if: connection identity is independent of IP/port
derivation_rules.why: TCP's identity is the 5-tuple. Change any element, the connection is a different one (to TCP). QUIC's connection ID survives 5-tuple changes. Mobile devices switching networks no longer drop connections — the user experience win.

derivation_rules.name: unambiguous_RTT_via_unique_packet_numbers
if: each packet has a unique number, including retransmits
derivation_rules.why: TCP's retransmits reuse sequence numbers, creating retransmission ambiguity (Karn's algorithm: don't use ambiguous RTTs). QUIC's unique packet numbers always give clean RTT samples. Better congestion control input.

derivation_rules.name: user_space_implementation_enables_rapid_iteration
if: the protocol implementation runs in user space
then: updates ship via application updates, not kernel updates
derivation_rules.why: TCP changes require kernel updates → years to deploy. QUIC's user-space implementations (Cloudflare quiche, Google's, Microsoft's MsQuic) deploy with browser/server updates — weeks. Critical for the protocol's rapid evolution.
